claim: In adult neurogenesis young neurons connect to the existing network via formation of thousands of new synapses.
source: In adult neurogenesis young neurons connect to the existing network via formation of thousands of new synapses.
evidence: This is a general statement about adult neurogenesis that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: At early developmental stages, glutamatergic synapses are sparse, immature and functionally 'silent', expressing mainly NMDA receptors.
source: At early developmental stages, glutamatergic synapses are sparse, immature and functionally 'silent', expressing mainly NMDA receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing NMDA-receptor dominance in young neurons (Figure 2) and by citations to prior work.

claim: In 2- to 3-week-old young neurons of adult mice, brief-burst activity in glutamatergic fibers is sufficient to induce postsynaptic AP firing in the absence of AMPA receptors.
source: Here we show in 2- to 3-week-old young neurons of adult mice, that brief-burst activity in glutamatergic fibers is sufficient to induce postsynaptic AP firing in the absence of AMPA receptors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing CNQX-insensitive AP firing in young neurons (Figure 4).

claim: The enhanced excitability of young neurons leads to efficient temporal summation of small NMDA currents.
source: The enhanced excitability of the young neurons lead to efficient temporal summation of small NMDA currents, dynamic unblocking of silent synapses and NMDA-receptor-dependent AP firing.
evidence: This is supported by data showing high EPSP/EPSC ratios and burst summation in young neurons (Figure 1).

claim: Young neurons show dynamic unblocking of silent synapses during brief-burst activity.
source: The enhanced excitability of the young neurons lead to efficient temporal summation of small NMDA currents, dynamic unblocking of silent synapses and NMDA-receptor-dependent AP firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that burst stimulation can evoke APs despite the presence of Mg2+ block at resting potential.

claim: Early synaptic inputs are powerfully converted into reliable spiking output in young neurons.
source: Therefore, early synaptic inputs are powerfully converted into reliable spiking output.
evidence: This is supported by data showing high firing probability in young neurons despite small synaptic currents (Figure 4).

claim: Due to high synaptic gain, small dendritic trees and sparse connectivity, neighboring young neurons are activated by different distinct subsets of afferent fibers with minimal overlap.
source: Furthermore, due to high synaptic gain, small dendritic trees and sparse connectivity, neighboring young neurons are activated by different distinct subsets of afferent fibers with minimal overlap.
evidence: This is supported by paired recording data showing minimal overlap in firing fields between neighboring young neurons (Figure 7).

claim: Synaptic recruitment of young neurons generates sparse and orthogonal AP firing.
source: Taken together, synaptic recruitment of young neurons generates sparse and orthogonal AP firing, which may support sparse coding during hippocampal information processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on narrow firing fields and minimal overlap between neighboring cells.

claim: Sparse and orthogonal firing in young neurons may support sparse coding during hippocampal information processing.
source: Taken together, synaptic recruitment of young neurons generates sparse and orthogonal AP firing, which may support sparse coding during hippocampal information processing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed firing patterns.

claim: During postnatal development, new synapse formation is initiated via activation of extrasynaptic NMDA receptors on dendritic shafts.
source: During postnatal development, new synapse formation is initiated via activation of extrasynaptic NMDA receptors on dendritic shafts and the first glutamatergic synapses are believed to form as 'silent synapses' lacking postsynaptic AMPA receptors (Durand et al., 1996; Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Maletic-Savatic et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The first glutamatergic synapses are believed to form as 'silent synapses' lacking postsynaptic AMPA receptors.
source: During postnatal development, new synapse formation is initiated via activation of extrasynaptic NMDA receptors on dendritic shafts and the first glutamatergic synapses are believed to form as 'silent synapses' lacking postsynaptic AMPA receptors (Durand et al., 1996; Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Maletic-Savatic et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In adult born neurons spine formation is dependent on NMDA receptors.
source: Similarly, in adult born neurons spine formation is dependent on NMDA receptors (Mu et al., 2015; Sultan et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The first glutamatergic synapses in adult-born neurons are mostly silent synapses expressing NMDA receptors but no AMPA-receptors.
source: The first glutamatergic synapses are mostly silent synapses expressing NMDA receptors but no AMPA-receptors (Chancey et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Early NMDA-only synapses are activated during learning and shape dendrite development as early as 1–2 weeks post mitosis.
source: These early NMDA-only synapses are activated during learning and shape dendrite development as early as 1–2 weeks post mitosis (Tronel et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The time window between 1–3 weeks after cell division is important for spine formation and constitutes a critical period for NMDA-dependent survival.
source: Consistent with this notion, the time window between 1–3 weeks after cell division is not only important for spine formation, it also constitutes a critical period for NMDA-dependent survival, as cell death during this period is strongly increased in newborn neurons with a genetic deletion of the NR1 NMDA receptor subunit (Tashiro et al., 2006, 2007; Mu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The AMPA component substantially increases during the following weeks and glutamatergic synapses induce AMPA-receptor dependent firing of APs after about 4 weeks post mitosis.
source: The AMPA component substantially increases during the following weeks and glutamatergic synapses induce AMPA-receptor dependent firing of APs after about 4 weeks post mitosis (Mongiat et al., 2009; Dieni et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Glutamatergic AP firing in young granule cells might be important to generate synaptic output and to support activity-dependent synaptic plasticity at input and output synapses.
source: Glutamatergic AP firing in young granule cells might be important to generate synaptic output, but also to support activity-dependent synaptic plasticity at input and output synapses (Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004; Ge et al., 2007; Bischofberger, 2007; Gu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Due to reduced GABAergic inhibition and cellular 'hyperexcitability' the young population might be active under many different behavioural conditions, not discriminating between different memory items.
source: Due to reduced GABAergic inhibition and cellular 'hyperexcitability' the young population might be active under many different behavioural conditions, not discriminating between different memory items (Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Danielson et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement describes a hypothesis from prior literature, supported by citations.

claim: Synapse-evoked firing is difficult to obtain in newborn neurons up to 4 weeks post mitosis, due to low excitatory synaptic connectivity.
source: On the other hand, it was claimed that synapse-evoked firing is difficult to obtain in newborn neurons up to 4 weeks post mitosis, due to low excitatory synaptic connectivity (Dieni et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement describes a claim from prior literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Behavioural data suggest a contribution of young neurons to hippocampus-dependent learning tasks already around ~3–4 weeks post mitosis.
source: In contrast, behavioural data suggest the opposite, indicating a contribution of young neurons to hippocampus-dependent learning tasks already around ~3–4 weeks post mitosis (Kee et al., 2007; Clelland et al., 2009; Kheirbek et al., 2012; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Gu et al., 2012), probably by improving pattern separation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Young neurons probably contribute to learning by improving pattern separation.
source: In contrast, behavioural data suggest the opposite, indicating a contribution of young neurons to hippocampus-dependent learning tasks already around ~3–4 weeks post mitosis (Kee et al., 2007; Clelland et al., 2009; Kheirbek et al., 2012; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Gu et al., 2012), probably by improving pattern separation.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited behavioral studies.

claim: At ~2–3 weeks newborn young granule cells generate input-specific sparse and orthogonal AP firing.
source: Here, we show that already at ~2–3 weeks newborn young granule cells generate input-specific sparse and orthogonal AP firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: At 2-3 weeks, young neurons form 'silent' synapses which are dynamically unblocked during brief burst-activity in presynaptic fibers.
source: At this stage they form 'silent' synapses which are dynamically unblocked during brief burst-activity in presynaptic fibers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing burst-evoked AP firing despite AMPA receptor blockade.

claim: Dynamic unblocking of silent synapses reliably induced NMDA-receptor dependent AP firing in young neurons.
source: This reliably induced NMDA-receptor dependent AP firing in the young neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing AP5-sensitive firing in young neurons.

claim: Young neurons can be excited by a small non-overlapping population of afferent glutamatergic fibers.
source: Finally, we used paired patch-clamp recordings in neighbouring granule cells to show that the young neurons can be excited by a small non-overlapping population of afferent glutamatergic fibers, well suited to support sparse coding of neuronal information already from 2 weeks post mitosis onwards.
evidence: This is supported by paired recording data showing minimal overlap in firing fields.

claim: The Rin of retrovirus labelled neurons was initially very high (~32 GΩ) at 7 days post injection.
source: Similar to previous data, the Rin of retrovirus labelled neurons (n = 77) was initially very high (~32 GΩ) at 7 days post injection (dpi), followed by a ~4 fold decay per week (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Rin of retrovirus labelled neurons showed a ~4 fold decay per week.
source: Similar to previous data, the Rin of retrovirus labelled neurons (n = 77) was initially very high (~32 GΩ) at 7 days post injection (dpi), followed by a ~4 fold decay per week (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements and fitting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mature granule cells showed large AMPA-receptor mediated EPSCs at −80 mV (1291 ± 304 pA, n = 7).
source: Whereas mature granule cells showed large AMPA-receptor mediated EPSCs at −80 mV (1291 ± 304 pA, n = 7), the synaptic currents in 2 wpi neurons were more than 100-fold smaller (3.3 ± 1.0 pA, n = 6).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: The synaptic currents in 2 wpi neurons were more than 100-fold smaller (3.3 ± 1.0 pA, n = 6) than in mature neurons.
source: Whereas mature granule cells showed large AMPA-receptor mediated EPSCs at −80 mV (1291 ± 304 pA, n = 7), the synaptic currents in 2 wpi neurons were more than 100-fold smaller (3.3 ± 1.0 pA, n = 6).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: The difference in EPSP amplitude between mature and 2-week-old cells was much less pronounced (13.9 ± 2.8 mV, n = 14 versus 3.2 ± 0.4 mV, n = 6).
source: By contrast the difference in EPSP amplitude between mature and 2-week-old cells was much less pronounced (13.9 ± 2.8 mV, n = 14 versus 3.2 ± 0.4 mV, n = 6)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from current-clamp recordings.

claim: The ratio between EPSP and EPSC was about 25-times larger at 2 wpi (2.17 ± 0.47 mV/pA, n = 6) compared to mature neurons (0.08 ± 0.01 mV/pA, n = 19).
source: and the ratio between EPSP and EPSC was about 25-times larger at 2 wpi (2.17 ± 0.47 mV/pA, n = 6) compared to mature neurons (0.08 ± 0.01 mV/pA, n = 19, Figure 1c).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Glutamatergic synapses can effectively depolarize newly generated granule cells younger than 3 weeks, although AMPA-receptor mediated synaptic currents are tiny.
source: Taken together, the data indicate that glutamatergic synapses can effectively depolarize newly generated granule cells younger than 3 weeks, although AMPA-receptor mediated synaptic currents are tiny.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EPSP/EPSC ratio data.

claim: Synaptic activity in the dentate gyrus in vivo is rhythmically patterned at theta-gamma frequencies.
source: Synaptic activity in the dentate gyrus in vivo is rhythmically patterned at theta-gamma frequencies (Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Newly generated cells at 2 wpi showed a burst EPSP amplitude of 30.2 ± 3.7 mV (n = 8) not significantly different from mature granule cells (29.8 ± 1.6 mV; n = 13, p=0.91).
source: On average, newly generated cells at 2 wpi showed a burst EPSP amplitude of 30.2 ± 3.7 mV (n = 8) not significantly different from mature granule cells (29.8 ± 1.6 mV; n = 13, p=0.91, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from current-clamp recordings with statistical comparison.

claim: EPSP size reaches 50% of mature levels at 1.9 GΩ, corresponding to an estimated age of about 3 weeks post mitosis.
source: Fitting the data with a sigmoidal decay indicates that EPSP size reaches 50% of mature levels at 1.9 GΩ, corresponding to an estimated age of about 3 weeks post mitosis.
evidence: This is derived from fitting experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Burst amplitude versus Rin was not significantly dependent on Rin as suggested by linear regression analysis (p=0.08).
source: By contrast, plotting the burst amplitude versus Rin, was not significantly dependent on Rin as suggested by linear regression analysis (p=0.08, Figure 1h).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The increase in synapse number is largely balanced by a concomitant (homeostatic) decrease in excitability and decrease in the impact of synaptic currents onto membrane depolarization.
source: This indicates that the increase in synapse number is largely balanced by a concomitant (homeostatic) decrease in excitability and decrease in the impact of synaptic currents onto membrane depolarization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that burst EPSP amplitudes are similar despite different synapse numbers.

claim: The ratio of the burst amplitude relative to single EPSPs was ~4 times larger at 2 wpi (9.57 ± 0.29, n = 11) compared to mature neurons (2.66 ± 0.14, n = 20, p<0.0001).
source: As single EPSPs were smaller in young cells, the ratio of the burst amplitude relative to single EPSPs was ~4 times larger at 2 wpi (9.57 ± 0.29, n = 11) compared to mature neurons (2.66 ± 0.14, n = 20, p<0.0001, Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Burst–EPSP ratios significantly correlate with the membrane time constant of young and mature GCs (p<0.0001, Spearman Correlation r = 0.83).
source: We further plotted burst–EPSP ratios against the membrane time constant measured in the very same neurons (Figure 1i,j), showing a significant correlation (p<0.0001, Spearman Correlation r = 0.83).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: The high membrane resistivity and associated slow membrane time constant contribute significantly to the effective temporal summation of EPSPs during brief burst activity.
source: This suggests that the high membrane resistivity and associated slow membrane time constant contribute significantly to the effective temporal summation of EPSPs during brief burst activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between burst-EPSP ratio and membrane time constant.

claim: An about 100-fold difference in EPSC-EPSP conversion in young neurons compensates for the much smaller synaptic currents to finally reach similar burst amplitudes in young and mature neurons.
source: These data show that an about 100-fold difference in EPSC-EPSP conversion in young neurons compensates for the much smaller synaptic currents to finally reach similar burst amplitudes in young and mature neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined EPSP/EPSC ratio and burst amplitude data.

claim: New glutamatergic synapses onto newborn young granule cells express a relatively high density of NMDA receptors and show a large NMDA-AMPA receptor ratio.
source: Using voltage-clamp recordings we confirmed that new glutamatergic synapses onto newborn young granule cells express a relatively high density of NMDA receptors and show a large NMDA-AMPA receptor ratio (Figure 2, Chancey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 2 and a citation to prior work.

claim: Slow NMDA-receptor mediated synaptic currents in the absence of AMPA-receptor currents constitute the typical finger print of 'silent synapses'.
source: Slow NMDA-receptor mediated synaptic currents in the absence of AMPA-receptor currents constitute the typical finger print of 'silent synapses'.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Silent synapses appear to be the predominant type of glutamatergic synapses in young neurons before 3 weeks of cell age.
source: This appears to be the predominant type of glutamatergic synapses in young neurons before 3 weeks of cell age (Figure 2a–e)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 showing high NMDA/AMPA ratios.

claim: NMDA currents in young cells at 2 wpi are about ~50 times smaller (9.2 ± 2.3 pA, n = 6) compared to mature neurons (414 ± 83 pA, n = 7, p<0.01).
source: Furthermore, NMDA currents in young cells at 2 wpi are about ~50 times smaller (9.2 ± 2.3 pA, n = 6) compared to mature neurons (414 ± 83 pA, n = 7, p<0.01), consistent with a low synapse density at 2 weeks (Figure 2c, Zhao et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Blocking NMDA receptors reduced the EPSP amplitude in young neurons by 53.6 ± 6.3% (n = 9, p<0.0001).
source: Remarkably, blocking NMDA receptors reduced the EPSP amplitude in young neurons by 53.6 ± 6.3% (n = 9, p<0.0001), while there was only a small and non-significant effect in mature granule cells (15.5 ± 6.2%, n = 5, p=0.069, Mann-Whitney, Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was only a small and non-significant effect of NMDA receptor blockade in mature granule cells (15.5 ± 6.2%, n = 5, p=0.069).
source: Remarkably, blocking NMDA receptors reduced the EPSP amplitude in young neurons by 53.6 ± 6.3% (n = 9, p<0.0001), while there was only a small and non-significant effect in mature granule cells (15.5 ± 6.2%, n = 5, p=0.069, Mann-Whitney, Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The relative open probability of NMDA receptors at −80 mV was about ~3% of maximum in both young and mature cells (3.2 ± 0.3% versus 3.3 ± 0.4% in 6 young and four mature cells, respectively, p=0.91).
source: The relative open probability at −80 mV extracted from the current-voltage relationship was about ~3% of maximum in both, young and mature cells (Figure 3de, 3.2 ± 0.3% versus 3.3 ± 0.4% in 6 young and four mature cells, respectively, p=0.91, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is calculated from I-V relationship data shown in Figure 3d-e.

claim: NMDAR-gating kinetic was slightly different, showing an about 1.6-fold slower decay time course in young versus mature neurons.
source: Furthermore, NMDAR-gating kinetic was slightly different, showing an about 1.6-fold slower decay time course in young versus mature neurons, which might be explained by the expression of GluN2B subunits in young versus GluN2A subunits in mature granule cells (Figure 3f, Chancey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The slower decay in young neurons might be explained by the expression of GluN2B subunits in young versus GluN2A subunits in mature granule cells.
source: Furthermore, NMDAR-gating kinetic was slightly different, showing an about 1.6-fold slower decay time course in young versus mature neurons, which might be explained by the expression of GluN2B subunits in young versus GluN2A subunits in mature granule cells (Figure 3f, Chancey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Although there is a normal Mg2+ block, the small but non-zero NMDA-conductance at resting membrane potential can depolarize young neurons due to high input resistance and slow membrane time constant.
source: This indicates that, although there is a normal Mg2+ block, the small but non-zero NMDA-conductance at resting membrane potential can depolarize young neurons due to high input resistance and slow membrane time constant.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the I-V relationship and EPSP contribution data.

claim: The number of glutamatergic synapses at 2 weeks is low, forming immature NMDA-receptor expressing 'silent' synapses.
source: These results show that the number of glutamatergic synapses at 2 weeks is low, forming immature NMDA-receptor expressing 'silent' synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the small NMDA current amplitudes and high NMDA/AMPA ratios.

claim: The intrinsic properties of young neurons promote membrane depolarizations by very small NMDA currents at the resting membrane potential.
source: However, the intrinsic properties of young neurons promote membrane depolarizations by very small NMDA currents at the resting membrane potential, resulting in dynamic unblocking of further synaptic NMDA-receptors during brief burst activity, finally leading to large synaptic potentials.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on high input resistance, NMDA contribution to EPSPs, and burst summation.

claim: The probability to evoke an AP via burst stimulation in cells with an estimated age of 2–3 weeks was only slightly smaller (88.4 ± 3.2%, n = 38, 30µA) compared to mature cells (100 ± 0%, n = 22, p=0.011).
source: Remarkably, the probability to evoke an AP via burst stimulation in cells with an estimated age of 2–3 weeks was only slightly smaller (88.4 ± 3.2%, n = 38, 30µA) compared to mature cells (100 ± 0%, n = 22, p=0.011, Mann-Whitney, Figure 4f)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Young neurons showed typically a single postsynaptic spike, whereas mature cells fired on average about three spikes per burst.
source: First, young neurons showed typically a single postsynaptic spike, whereas mature cells fired on average about three spikes per burst (Figure 4ab).
evidence: This is a direct observation from current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Spike amplitude was smaller in young neurons (108.5 ± 2.5 mV, n = 21) than in mature cells (143.3 ± 1.3 mV, n = 5, p<0.0001).
source: Second, spike amplitude was smaller in young neurons (108.5 ± 2.5 mV, n = 21) than in mature cells (143.3 ± 1.3 mV, n = 5, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from current-clamp recordings.

claim: Half-duration of spikes was longer in young (5.2 ± 0.8 ms, n = 21) versus mature cells (1.6 ± 0.1 ms, n = 5, p<0.0001).
source: Third, half-duration of spikes was longer in young (5.2 ± 0.8 ms, n = 21) versus mature cells (1.6 ± 0.1 ms, n = 5, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from current-clamp recordings.

claim: The lower density of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels in young versus mature neurons is consistent with the smaller and broader spikes.
source: Third, half-duration of spikes was longer in young (5.2 ± 0.8 ms, n = 21) versus mature cells (1.6 ± 0.1 ms, n = 5, p<0.0001). These results are consistent with the notion that the density of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels is lower in the young versus mature neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spike properties.

claim: Spiking in young cells started with longer delay (98 ± 9 ms, n = 21) than in mature cells (45 ± 7 ms, n = 5, p<0.0001), relative to stimulation onset.
source: Finally, spiking in young cells started with longer delay (98 ± 9 ms, n = 21) than in mature cells (45 ± 7 ms, n = 5, p<0.0001), relative to stimulation onset, consistent with the slow membrane time constant and prolonged temporal summation of EPSPs in young neurons.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from current-clamp recordings.

claim: Single stimuli with high intensity could evoke APs in mature granule cells, but never induced spiking in young neurons with Rin above 2 GΩ.
source: Notably, single stimuli with high intensity could evoke APs in mature granule cells, but never induced spiking in young neurons with Rin above 2 GΩ (data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments.

claim: Application of CNQX blocked burst-evoked AP firing in mature neurons.
source: Whereas application of CNQX blocked burst-evoked AP firing in mature neurons, spiking was largely unaffected in 2- to 3 week old cells generating 1.28 ± 0.11 and 1.34 ± 0.15 APs per burst in control and CNQX, respectively (p=0.69, n = 16, Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct observation from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Spiking was largely unaffected in 2- to 3 week old cells by CNQX, generating 1.28 ± 0.11 and 1.34 ± 0.15 APs per burst in control and CNQX, respectively (p=0.69, n = 16).
source: Whereas application of CNQX blocked burst-evoked AP firing in mature neurons, spiking was largely unaffected in 2- to 3 week old cells generating 1.28 ± 0.11 and 1.34 ± 0.15 APs per burst in control and CNQX, respectively (p=0.69, n = 16, Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The most important component in young cells is provided by NMDA receptors, as application of AP5 largely blocked AP generation.
source: However, the most important component in young cells is provided by NMDA receptors, as application of AP5 largely blocked AP generation (Figure 4c–e).
evidence: This is a direct observation from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mature granule cells still fired APs in AP5 in response to burst stimulation with high success rate.
source: By contrast, mature granule cells still fired APs in AP5 in response to burst stimulation with high success rate (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a direct observation from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The number of spikes per burst in mature cells was reduced in AP5 (1.12 ± 0.23 versus 3.16 ± 0.39, n = 5, p=0.0011).
source: The number of spikes per burst, however, was reduced (1.12 ± 0.23 versus 3.16 ± 0.39, n = 5, p=0.0011).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from pharmacological experiments.

claim: AP firing on fully connected mature granule cells is critically dependent on strong AMPA-receptor activation with some modulation by NMDA receptors.
source: These results show that AP firing on fully connected mature granule cells is critically dependent on strong AMPA-receptor activation with some modulation by NMDA receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: In young neurons NMDA receptors are critically important and silent synapses can be dynamically unsilenced by brief-burst activity to reliably evoke AP firing in absence of AMPA receptors.
source: By contrast, in young neurons NMDA receptors are critically important and silent synapses can be dynamically unsilenced by brief-burst activity to reliably evoke AP firing in absence of AMPA receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological experiments showing CNQX-insensitive but AP5-sensitive firing.

claim: The lower synapse number in young cells is balanced by the enhanced intrinsic excitability.
source: Again, this supports the conclusion, that the lower synapse number in young cells is balanced by the enhanced intrinsic excitability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that firing probability is similar despite different synapse numbers.

claim: Enhanced intrinsic excitability can generate glutamatergic AP firing in young cells with similar probability as in mature granule cells despite a more than 100-fold difference in EPSC amplitude at resting membrane potential.
source: Remarkably, this can generate glutamatergic AP firing in young cells with similar probability as in mature granule cells despite a more than 100-fold difference in EPSC amplitude at resting membrane potential.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on EPSC amplitudes and firing probabilities.

claim: The diameter of the dendritic cone was on average 4-fold smaller in young (86 ± 15 µm, n = 8) versus mature neurons (324 ± 17 µm, n = 7, p=0.0003).
source: The diameter of the dendritic cone was on average 4-fold smaller in young (86 ± 15 µm, n = 8) versus mature neurons (324 ± 17 µm, n = 7, p=0.0003).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from morphological analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The height of the cone was smaller in young (127 ± 13 µm) than in mature cells (188 ± 12 µm, p=0.0037).
source: Furthermore, the height of the cone was smaller in young (127 ± 13 µm) than in mature cells (188 ± 12 µm, p=0.0037) suggesting that the total cone volume is substantially smaller in the young neurons.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from morphological analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The total cone volume is substantially smaller in the young neurons.
source: Furthermore, the height of the cone was smaller in young (127 ± 13 µm) than in mature cells (188 ± 12 µm, p=0.0037) suggesting that the total cone volume is substantially smaller in the young neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the diameter and height measurements.

claim: The chance that an entorhinal afferent fiber might target a specific young neuron is much smaller than for a given mature cell.
source: This indicates that the chance that an entorhinal afferent fiber might target a specific young neuron is much smaller than for a given mature cell.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the smaller dendritic tree volume.

claim: Stimulation sites that successfully induced spike discharge were spatially much more restricted in DCX-DsRed positive young neurons relative to mature granule cells.
source: As shown in Figure 6a–c, stimulation sites that successfully induced spike discharge were spatially much more restricted in DCX-DsRed positive young neurons relative to mature granule cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The half-width of the dendritic 'firing field' was about 5-times more narrow in young neurons than in mature granule cells (76.7 ± 8.1 µm versus 360.8 ± 70.6 µm in n = 15 and n = 11 cells, p<0.0001).
source: On average, the half-width of the dendritic 'firing field' was about 5-times more narrow in young neurons than in mature granule cells (76.7 ± 8.1 µm versus 360.8 ± 70.6 µm in n = 15 and n = 11 cells, p<0.0001, Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from experiments shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The broad firing field in mature cells is consistent with a large amplitude of synaptic currents, a relatively large dendritic tree and several thousand spines and excitatory glutamatergic synapses present on dendrites of a mature granule cell.
source: The broad firing field in mature cells is consistent with a large amplitude of synaptic currents, a relatively large dendritic tree and several thousand spines and excitatory glutamatergic synapses present on dendrites of a mature granule cell (Zhao et al., 2006; Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior morphological studies.

claim: The efficient conversion of small EPSCs into membrane depolarization in young cells allows for glutamatergic AP firing induced by the small subset of presynaptic fibers synapsing onto the small dendritic tree of these neurons.
source: By contrast, the efficient conversion of small EPSCs into membrane depolarization in young cells allows for glutamatergic AP firing induced by the small subset of presynaptic fibers synapsing onto the small dendritic tree of these neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on narrow firing fields and high EPSC-EPSP conversion.
